title: Covington at the Point

bodyMarkdown:
[Covington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covington,_Kentucky) grew up on "the Point," the land where the Licking River meets the Ohio. Across the Ohio lies Cincinnati, and across the Licking lies [Newport](/stories/newport-at-the-licking-mouth/).

## Thomas Kennedy's land

[Thomas Kennedy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Covington,_Kentucky) is recognized as the area's first permanent white settler. He came from Pennsylvania around 1790, landing first at Cincinnati. He then bought 200 acres stretching from the Licking River to the Ohio and ran a ferry there.

## Founding the town

In 1814 John Gano, Richard Gano and Thomas Carneal bought 150 acres at the Point from Kennedy for $50,000. They laid out the town the next year and organized lot sales to draw settlers. The town was named for Gen. Leonard Covington, a Maryland-born officer killed at the Battle of Crysler's Farm in the War of 1812. The Kentucky General Assembly incorporated Covington in February 1815.

Growth was slow at first. A cotton factory opened by 1828, and the population reached 743 by 1830. The legislature raised Covington to city status in 1834. Kenton County, named for pioneer Simon Kenton, was created on January 29, 1840.

## River city

German immigrants arrived in large numbers after 1830. Like Cincinnati, Covington's factories and businesses were heavily staffed by Catholic and German immigrants. The city became a center for tobacco and cigar production. Stewart Iron Works, founded in 1862, was for a time the largest iron fence maker in the world. Distilleries, glassworks and stove factories followed.

During the Civil War, Union forces built fortifications nearby, including Fort Wright and Fort Mitchell. In late summer 1862 about 8,000 Confederate troops under Gen. Henry Heth approached but did not engage in significant fighting. In 1867 the [John A. Roebling Suspension Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Roebling_Suspension_Bridge) linked Covington directly to Cincinnati.

The Census Bureau placed the country's center of population at Covington for the 1880 census. By 1900 it was Kentucky's second-largest city and industrial center, with almost 43,000 people.

## Kentucky today

Covington declined during the Great Depression and the mid-20th century, and the 1937 Ohio River flood caused heavy damage. Redevelopment has followed since the late 20th century. With a population of 40,961 in the 2020 census, it is the largest city in Northern Kentucky. Historic districts such as MainStrasse Village preserve its German heritage near the old Point.
